**Abstract (`r manuscript_stats$abstract_words` words)**

Biodiversity is under pressure from multiple global change drivers including climate change, pollution, and land-use change. Theory suggests that several of these drivers affect plant diversity through their impacts on plant community biomass. We hypothesize that by using community biomass as a common currency, we can arrive at a more synthetic understanding of the effects of multiple global change drivers on plant diversity. We test this hypothesis in a replicated field experiment in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, simulating the effects of climate warming, nitrogen addition, and grazing. Our study showed that these global change drivers operated indeed on diversity through community biomass, but more strongly in the temperature and nutrient limited alpine site. In the warmer sub-alpine site, warming and nitrogen can directly override the biomass-mediated effects. Using environmental affinities to describe the change in environmental niches of the plant communities revealed a useful approach to understand the underlying mechanisms.
